meta.title: How Does Fox News Frame the WNBA?
meta.description: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association
meta.hed: How Does Fox News Frame the WNBA?
meta.dek: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association
meta.headerImg: wnba-framed.png | The WNBA logo hung inside an empty gilt picture frame

content.value: I’ve loved and played (mediocre) basketball all my life, but I only became a WNBA fan when I moved to Seattle five years ago. (Let’s go, Storm.) Since then, I’ve become a bit obsessed. I’ve also become fixated on a question. Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA, too?

fox-iran-wnba.png | Fox News homepage navigation listing its Hot Topics: War With Iran, then WNBA Controversy | A screenshot from the Fox News home page in August 2026. Their hottest topics: literal war and women’s basketball.
This question dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t read or watch Fox News myself.

The first clue came at a family gathering. I was chatting with an older conservative family member, who, out of the blue, started name-dropping WNBA players, saying praiseworthy things about superstar Caitlin Clark and suspect things about other Black players.
This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.

value.caption: Fox News clips from Riley Gaines on Hannity, The Will Cain Show, and Clay Travis on The Ingraham Angle.

content.value: The second clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, my Google Chrome app recommended more WNBA news. That made sense. But then I started getting served coverage from, of all places, Fox News. Wait… what?
I saw dozens of Fox News takes on women’s basketball, often with a clear political bias, and an implicitly racist and homophobic framing.

clips: June 2026 | pink | Who is Alyssa Thomas? ((Alyssa Thomas|face))WNBA star suspended for punching Caitlin Clark ((Caitlin Clark|face)) in the throat
January 2025 | green | WNBA star ((DiJonai Carrington|face)) who hurt Caitlin Clark's ((Caitlin Clark|face)) eye calls for league to take action against Trump administration policies
May 2025 | pink | Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese ((Angel Reese|face)) a jacka-- for jealousy of Caitlin Clark ((Caitlin Clark|face)) in response to ESPN analyst

content.value: Headline after headline pit the league’s most famous straight white star, Clark, against other WNBA players, mainly Black and/or queer women, like Alyssa Thomas, DiJonai Carrington, or Angel Reese.

When it comes to sports, there are, at least seemingly, facts. This team won, and this team lost. This player scored a lot of points. You would expect a lot of similar coverage. But these headlines were clearly different.
So I decided to collect some data.  How does Fox News cover the WNBA compared to everybody else?

steps.text: Let’s start with headlines. If all outlets mentioned Caitin Clark equally, she would be here in the middle.
But Fox News mentions Clark 3.2x more than other outlets.
steps.clip: race | July 2026 | pink | CNN's Abby Phillip claims GOP lawmakers back ==Caitlin Clark== exclusively because she is White

steps.text: Here’s where the other players stand.
Fox often pairs Clark with—and against—Angel Reese.
Of players on the Indiana Fever, Clark’s team, Fox highlights white players like Sophie Cunningham up to 7.8x more...
…while covering Black players like Aliyah Boston and Kelsey Mitchell up to 1.3x less.

Even though Boston and Mitchell have been extraordinary on the court.

In 2026, Mitchell broke the WNBA record for most consecutive games with 20+ points.

steps.names: A’ja Wilson, Napheesa Collier, Breanna Stewart
steps.text: Fox News discusses all-stars like Napheesa Collier, Breanna Stewart, and A’ja Wilson approximately 3-5x less than other outlets...

steps.names: DiJonai Carrington, Natasha Cloud, Brittney Griner
steps.text: while talking about DiJonai Carrington, Natasha Cloud, and Brittney Griner as much as 4.9x more.
steps.clip: Sun's ==DiJonai Carrington== sends fiery message to fans after appearing to take swipe at Caitlin Clark.

content.value: Why does Fox News talk about Carrington, Cloud, and Griner so much?
DiJonai Carrington, Natasha Cloud, Brittney Griner

It’s political. These players’ vocal leftist views—on race, gender, Black Lives Matter (BLM) and more—make them a target for conservative coverage of the WNBA, which has long sought to frame the league as both dangerously radical and illegitimate.

For example, Carrington has publicly criticized Clark for not being vocal enough in denouncing her racist and bigoted fans. She has fouled Clark and Cunningham in high-profile ways. And she’s made it clear that she doesn’t like Trump.

clips: Sun's DiJonai Carrington ((DiJonai Carrington|face)) sends fiery message to fans after appearing to take swipe at Caitlin Clark.
Jan 2025 | WNBA star DiJonai Carrington ((DiJonai Carrington|face))  flaunts explicit message on pre-game outfit directed at President Trump
Brittney Griner  ((Brittney Griner|face)) is coming home. Will she stand for the anthem now that she's back in the USA?
WNBA player Natasha Cloud ((Natasha Cloud|face)) calls out Israel on Oct 7 while blaming Republicans for government shutdown

content.value: Cloud’s outspoken activism—for BLM, Gaza, trans rights, and more—has also been a focal point. Meanwhile, Griner was imprisoned in Russia in 2022, making her a consistent subject of news. But she is often criticized for her progressive views, too, and Fox has helped to stoke conspiracy theories about her gender identity, suggesting that she is a man.
It’s no coincidence that these are all queer Black women, too.

steps.text: On TV, Fox talks more about Clark ((Caitlin Clark| face)) and Cunningham ((Sophie Cunningham| face)) than other outlets, too.
This is cable news coverage of the WNBA, via their chyrons—you know, those headlines that appear at the bottom of your screen.
Fox News talks incessantly about fouls against Clark. This is a kind of dog whistle, as I will explain later.

steps.groups: alyssa, thomas // dijonai, carrington //  napheesa, collier // paige, bueckers
steps.text:
For other players, we see nearly the same breakdown as the online coverage.

Carrington ((DiJonai Carrington| face)) and Thomas ((Alyssa Thomas| face)) lean more Fox, while Bueckers ((Paige Bueckers| face)) and Collier ((Napheesa Collier| face)) lean more other outlets.
Search any term.

content.value: In the summer of 2026, the right-wing politicization of the WNBA burst into the mainstream.

In July, Sophie Cunningham ((Sophie Cunningham|face))—Clark’s teammate and on-court “bodyguard”—made anti-trans remarks. While she told ESPN that she “got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans” and clarified that “I never once said that," she also expressed a desire to “protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men"—using the exact language and hateful agenda items of the anti-trans movement. She later doubled down on those comments.
This inspired right-wing politicians and anti-trans advocates around the world to rally around her, including Vice President J.D. Vance, infamous literary TERF J.K. Rowling, and grifter Jennifer Sey.
vance-cunningham-fox.png | Fox News segment showing Vice President J.D. Vance praising Sophie Cunningham | Vice President J.D. Vance praises Sophie Cunningham on Fox News, August 2026.

Trans women’s participation in the WNBA has become a non-stop Fox News talking point. They’ve spent more than 13 hours (!) discussing the WNBA this summer alone. It’s worth repeating: no transgender players are currently in the league. As Fox News pundit Jesse Watters recently said on air: “We have to do this again, really? Someone wore a t-shirt at a WNBA game? This isn’t a news story…. We don’t even cover the NBA. Why are we covering the WNBA?”
How did professional women’s basketball—a league that, for decades, most people didn’t watch or care anything about—transform into a mainstream political lightning rod?

Despite the recent attention, it didn’t happen overnight. And the media, especially conservative media, played a key role. So let’s dive into the data and see how Fox News has framed the WNBA as a hot-button culture war issue—one that was primed, at the right moment, to explode.
Fightin’ Words
It’s not just the amount of attention that Fox devotes to the WNBA. It’s also the language they use.

steps.text:
Here’s how Fox’s vocabulary differs from other outlets when reporting on the WNBA.

This is a method (aptly) called “fightin’ words,” which shows the most distinctive words used by one group vs. another.

steps.words: Caitlin Clark, Sophie Cunningham, Angel Reese, DiJonai Carrington, Breanna Stewart, lynx, liberty, aces
steps.text:
You can see Fox’s outsized focus on Clark, Cunningham, Reese, and Carrington...

…and the relative neglect of players like Stewie (Breanna Stewart) or other leading teams (Aces, Liberty).

steps.words: social media, white privilege, hard foul, collective bargaining, biological men, transgender athletes, white house, fever star, points rebounds, free agency
steps.text:
Fox consistently uses culture war phrases like ”white privilege” (derogatorily) and ”biological men” (referring to trans women). They talk excessively about hard fouls, as well as players’ comments on social media.

Meanwhile, other outlets talk about the WNBA’s collective bargaining or actual strategy and game play, like free agency, and points and rebounds.
Search any word or phrase.

content.value: What about language around specific players, like Clark?  ((Caitlin Clark|face))

This is a juicy question because there is currently a “fight over Caitlin Clark’s soul,” as University of Washington professor Kate Starbird, a leading misinformation researcher and former WNBA player, put it to me.

When Clark joined the league in 2024, the WNBA culture war debates really heated up. Some commentators noted that Clark’s background as a straight, white, Midwestern star may play a role in her broad appeal—a point that conservatives and Fox News pundits have rejected.

clark-fever-spurlock.jpg | Caitlin Clark, seen from behind in her white Indiana Fever number 22 jersey, releases a jump shot toward the basket. | Photo by Brian Spurlock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
But Clark is not a “stable” figure for the conservative or liberal media, Starbird said. And it’s not totally clear what her legacy will be.

One factor in the mix: social media. Starbid has previously written about the increasing pressure athletes feel to take political stances, especially from their large social media audiences. “The real risk for internet influencers—a class of celebrities that increasingly includes professional athletes—isn’t ‘falling down rabbit holes,’ but being ‘captured’ and radicalized by their audiences,” Starbird says. This is a potential risk for everyone from Clark to Cunningham to Carrington and beyond.

The point is that, at least right now, Clark is often talked about more than she talks. And, sometimes for that reason, the conservative media often uses her as a pawn. Let’s take a closer look at the coverage.

steps.text: This is the same approach applied per player, and broken down by sentence part.
steps.title: What happens to Caitlin Clark

steps.words: target, poke, shove, knock, strike, hit, punch
steps.text:
Here’s what happens to Clark, according to Fox News.

She is poked, targeted, hit, punched, struck, shoved, and knocked down.

They emphasize her rough treatment much more than other outlets.
Clark is a white phenom but also a victim and a target.
steps.title: How Fox News describes Caitlin Clark

steps.words: average, play, lead, win, clothesline, foul, poke, commit, foul

Explore any player.

content.value: You can see the divergent framing even with specific incidents.

For example, The Athletic opened a September 2024 piece about a DiJonai Carrington foul on Clark by downplaying it. They specifically emphasized that Clark downplayed it and made clear it wasn’t potential. By contrast, Fox News opened with a dramatic scene of Carrington sticking her “long fingernail” into Clark’s eye, and buried Clark’s comments many paragraphs later.

slides.outletText: Caitlin Clark downplayed being poked in the eye by Connecticut Sun guard DiJonai Carrington in Sunday’s WNBA first-round playoff loss, saying her eye “feels good…” “It wasn’t intentional by any means,” Clark said Tuesday. “You just watched the play, it wasn’t intentional.”
slides.foxText: Connecticut Sun guard DiJonai Carrington stuck her long fingernail in Caitlin Clark's eye during the Sun's 93-69 win over the Indiana Fever Sunday in the WNBA playoffs… Slow-motion footage showed Carrington bending her hand while coming down from the block attempt, pointing her nails in Clark's face.

slides.outletText: Cunningham wrapped her up with a hard foul and threw her to the ground, sparking a scuffle between the teams. Cunningham's foul was upgraded to a Flagrant 2, which comes with an automatic ejection, and Sheldon and Sun guard Lindsay Allen were both ejected as well.
slides.foxText: Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham received praise on social media Tuesday night as she appeared to defend Caitlin Clark with a hard foul on Connecticut Sun guard Jacy Sheldon… As the Fever put away the Sun 88-71, Cunningham was congratulated for stepping up as the team’s enforcer.

slides.outletText: The WNBA upgraded a foul committed by Chennedy Carter against Caitlin Clark to a Flagrant 1 after the league reviewed the check that became a talking point of Saturday’s game between the Indiana Fever and Chicago Sky.
slides.foxText: Sky guard Chennedy Carter was seen hip-checking Clark during the game, and her Sky teammate, Angel Reese, clapped for the hard foul that turned into a flagrant 1 violation after the WNBA reviewed it on Sunday.

slides.outletText: Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas has received a flagrant foul 2 penalty and a one-game suspension for "recklessly making contact with her fist to the throat area" of Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark, the WNBA announced Thursday… "We have a generational talent and WNBA superstar who had two cheap shots [against her] right there that weren't called," White said. "Absolutely unacceptable."
slides.foxText: Alyssa Thomas' thug-like play, punching Caitlin Clark in the throat and kneeing her in the groin, is indefensible. The league thought so, and so does the sane general public, who saw the WNBA’s biggest star mugged on the court like she was the victim of some schoolyard bullying.

content.value: You can see similar moments if you flip through the coverage.
The Fox News-WNBA Expanded Universe

Of course, Clark didn’t become Fox’s golden child white savior of the WNBA overnight. And their right-wing spin on women’s basketball didn’t start recently. It’s been a long (if evolving) game, with a rotating cast of characters.
To stoke controversy, Fox often stages conflict between individuals in click-bait headlines—either between extreme outside voices and WNBA players, or between the WNBA players themselves.
Let’s look at the web they’re been spinning.

steps.text: Each face is someone Fox News named in a WNBA headline. A line means two of them shared a headline.
Even before Clark entered the league, Fox’s coverage was hyper-political. They were bent on portraying the league as suspiciously liberal and radical.

steps.focus: Joe Biden, Megan Rapinoe, Sue Bird
steps.text: They underscored connections between the players’ 2020 BLM activism and then-President Joe Biden, and between point guard Sue Bird (and her then-girlfriend Megan Rapinoe) and Democrats.
steps.headline: Biden praises WNBA champs for social justice activism | Sue Bird, Megan Rapinoe attempt to dial up support for Democrats before Election Day |

steps.text: They dramatized conflict between Lebron James and Kelly Loeffler, a former WNBA owner and former senator. In 2021, she was defeated by Democrat Raphael Warnock, in part thanks to WNBA player advocacy.
steps.headline: LeBron James suggests buying WNBA team from Georgia Sen. Kelly Loeffler after projected loss

steps.text: In 2022, Brittney Griner became the central WNBA focal point, because she was arrested and imprisoned in Russia. The league was suddenly imbricated with broader world politics.

After Griner was freed in a prisoner swap, Fox notably turned to Donald Trump to suggest it was a bad deal.

He plainly devalued her life—and so did Fox by consistently platforming this framing.
steps.headline: Trump: Brittney Griner prisoner swap for 'Merchant of Death'  doesn't seem like a very good trade

steps.text: Then, in 2024, Clark joined the WNBA and fully took the spotlight.
She was often pit against Reese.

steps.focus: Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese, Dave Portnoy
steps.text: To foster animosity, Fox News turned to people like Dave Portnoy (Barstool Sports).
steps.headline: Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese a 'jacka--' for 'jealousy' of Caitlin Clark in response to ESPN analyst

steps.text: Steadily, Sophie Cunningham rose to prominence in the network, becoming the second largest node in 2026.
At the same time, Fox increasingly platformed anti-trans advocates like Enes Kanter Freedom and Riley Gaines.
Here’s all the people they were paired with.

content.value: “Rejecting” Identity Politics
This network isn’t just a collection of people. It’s organized around a particular way of seeing the WNBA—namely, through identity and political conflict.

Fox News vociferously rejects “identity politics” in WNBA coverage—the reference of social categories like race, gender, or sexuality, and the idea that political issues may be organized around them. But Fox News writers and pundits trade in (white) identity politics more than just about everyone.

everything's-racist-fox.png | Laura Ingraham and Clay Travis, founder of OutKick, discussing Clark on Fox News. | In this clip, Laura Ingraham and Clay Travis—the founder of OutKick—discuss a USA Today column that suggested some of Clark’s fans were racist and that fouls against her were being weaponized.

Bobby Burack, writing for Fox’s OutKick, recently criticized ESPN for being “racial idolaters” in their reporting about Clark. There is a false narrative, he claimed, that Clark is only a star “because America has starved for a straight white girl to save them from a league of largely black LGBTQ women.” He concluded: “ESPN ought to add some diversity to its WNBA commentary—diversity of opinion, that is.”

The irony is that Fox News talks more about race, gender, and identity in the WNBA than any other outlet, and about twice as much as ESPN. They’ve mentioned race or racial politics in 21% of their WNBA articles, on average, and in 34% this year.

Though Fox News claims that everybody else is talking about racism, they’re the ones talking about it the most, including on TV. Eighty-four percent of the time “racist” appeared in a WNBA chyron, it was on Fox News.

value.note: Cable news chyrons, {period}, from the Internet Archive’s Third Eye.

content.value: Across all the outlets, discussion of race and racial justice peaked in 2020. This is true for Fox, too. And it’s an important moment to return to.

wnba-blm-2020.jpg | Minnesota Lynx players standing with linked arms, wearing “Say Her Name” shirts | Minnesota Lynx players wear “Say Her Name” shirts and link arms in honor of Breonna Taylor before a game in July 2020. Phelan M. Ebenhack/AP

In 2020, WNBA players engaged in highly visible protest in support of BLM. They walked off the court during the national anthem and wore BLM and “Say Her Name” shirts on national television. They also successfully campaigned for Warnock, a Democrat, to win a U.S. Senate seat, defeating Atlanta Dream co-owner Loeffler, who was loudly opposed to players’ activism.

clips: July 2020 | green | Sen. Kelly Loeffler, co-owner of Atlanta Dream, ==objects to WNBA's social justice plans==
July 2020 | green | WNBA players ==walk off court during national anthem== ahead of season opener
July 2020 | green | WNBA players call on league to ==stop playing national anthem== before games
August 2020 | green | WNBA team wears shirts with ==Jacob Blake's name==, league postpones games following Kenosha shooting

content.value: All this was frequently covered by Fox, and often framed in implicitly disapproving terms. However, unlike other outlets, Fox News continued to make race a focal point after 2020, especially in relation to “race baiting” and “race bullies” around Clark.

clips: May 2026 | The WNBA won't grow this season if mean girls and race bullies refuse to accept Caitlin Clark
July 2026 | Alveda King slams USA Today columnist for invoking Emmett Till in Caitlin Clark piece: 'Pure race-baiting'
July 2026 | Stacey Dales provides much-needed logic to ESPN's Caitlin Clark coverage, dismantles race-baiter on set
May 2026 | Dakich: sports media has created an ‘industry’ out of complaining about white athletes like Caitlin Clark
May 2025 | Wings' Paige Bueckers laments lack of 'equal coverage' of Black women, talks 'White privilege'

content.value: If you look at the words most associated with “race” in Fox’s vocabulary, in fact, it’s race bullies, race idolaters, and race war.

While LGBTQ+ topics were mentioned less frequently overall, Fox News mentioned them in 13% of WNBA articles overall and in 37% of WNBA articles in 2026. That’s far more, proportionally, than any other outlet.

value.note: Cable news chyrons, {period}, from the Internet Archive’s Third Eye.

content.value: Fox’s obsession with race and with transgender women are not disconnected. They are, in fact, intimately connected. By dramatizing the danger posed to Clark, and the reverse white racism she supposedly faces, Fox News riles up their base against the broader WNBA, which includes not only many Black women but many gay and queer women, too. (According to a recent Atlantic article by Jemele Hill, the league is approximately 70 percent Black, and somewhere between 25 to 35 percent queer).

In a further twist, Fox News often highlights white players who conform to traditional conventions of femininity—like Cunningham, Kelsey Plum, or Cameron Brink—and denigrates Black players who do not, advancing conceptions of ideal (straight white femme) womanhood. Drawing these boundaries has only one obvious end: hating women, including trans women.

One particularly powerful WNBA narrative—which arguably ties both implicit racism and transphobia together—is about fouls. From the moment Clark entered the WNBA until today, conservatives have pushed a story that other players are fouling and purposely targeting her, often suggesting because she is white. This ramped up to the point that in July 2026 a group of Republican politicians literally sent a letter to the WNBA commissioner.
letter.jpeg | Letter from Republicans to the WNBA commissioner | Letter from Republicans to the WNBA commissioner

The politicians threatened that "if discrimination or retaliation is occurring and creating a hostile work environment” in the WNBA, then they would call for an “investigation by the Department of Justice, the Department of Labor, or the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission." They warned that the fouls against Clark might violate “federal civil rights laws.”

The Republicans cite, as evidence, the fact that “Clark has been hip-checked, poked in the eye, and struck in the throat during games.” Who emphasized exactly these points for months and months? Fox News.
Across more than two hundred articles, Fox News mentioned these exact words in the lead-up to the July 2026 letter.
You can also see that this physical contact was hammered home on cable TV.
So much so that even chyrons—the most condensed breaking news summaries—specifically included these terms.

This coverage matters. Republican politicians, including Trump, watch Fox News regularly and are influenced by it, as extensive reporting has shown. Fox News is also a node in a more diffuse network of right-wing blogs that have jumped on the WNBA bandwagon as of late.
Let’s Not Get Played

As we’ve seen, Fox News has fanned the flames of the WNBA culture war for years—through their emphasis on certain players over (and against) others, through their use of language, focus on certain topics, and framing of events. Their reporting laid the groundwork for what we’ve seen this summer: the seizure of the WNBA as a right-wing issue.

In 2026, Fox News discussed the WNBA more than ever. Thirty percent of this coverage mentioned trans athletes or issues, far outstripping other outlets. Many of these articles panic over transgender women playing in the WNBA (even though no transgender women are playing in the WNBA).

value.title: WNBA articles about trans athletes, 2026
value.note: Share of each outlet's 2026 WNBA articles that mention trans athletes or issues.

content.value: As Jesse Watters recently said on air, “Why are we covering the WNBA?” Or, more pointedly, “This is something I don’t care about.” He said the quiet part out loud. Fox News doesn’t actually care about women’s basketball. Right-wing pundits and politicians are using the WNBA to push their own agendas.

Sports are political. They have always been political. Throughout American history, athletes have been able to use their platforms to advocate for justice. And players in the WNBA are a great example of that.
jacob-blake.png | Julio Aguilar / Getty Images | Julio Aguilar / Getty Images
But we should be wary of how narratives about the WNBA are being framed by the right-wing media and outside parties who have little to no actual investment in the league.

When I went to my first WNBA game, I was shocked by how inclusive it felt. Black, queer, and POC women were celebrated on and off the court, as well on the jumbotron and in the stands. The dancers were teenaged girls doing sick hip-hop moves in baggy pants. The Storm’s goofy mascot, Doppler, uses they/them pronouns. Fox News-types like to make hell of things like that (and, in fact, they have). But the whole vibe was—and is—truly so nice, welcoming, and fun. It is completely different from every other (men’s) professional sporting event I have ever been to.

I don’t know how the WNBA will handle all of this increased attention—from the media, politicians, activists, trolls, new fans, and (unfortunately) my conservative relatives. The new WNBA commissioner certainly has their work cut out for them.

But I know one thing for sure. The version of the WNBA presented by Fox News is not recognizable to me. We need to see this framing for what it is, and push back against it, lest we all get played. Let’s not get played.

Data & Methods

Headlines and Articles. I collected any Fox News article (both headline and full text) that mentioned the WNBA or its players from 2019-2026. This corpus includes coverage from Outkick, now owned by Fox and published on their site.
As a comparison, I collected parallel WNBA coverage from ESPN, USA Today, CBS Sports, The Athletic (owned by the New York Times), and Just Women’s Sports.

TV Chyrons. I gathered nine years worth of cable news chyrons from Fox, MSNBC, and CNN, drawing on data from the Internet Archive's Third Eye OCR feed, and inspired by a very cool analysis by Charlie Smart.
Fightin Words. The word comparisons use “fightin’ words” aka weighted log-odds with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn 2008).
You can find data and code on GitHub.
